--- title: "Propensity-based methods" format: revealjs: slide-level: 2 incremental: true slide-number: true controls: true autoScale: true minScale: 0.6 maxScale: 1.0 center: false margin: 0.05 css: styles.css html-math-method: method: mathjax url: https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js mathjax: macros: independent: "\\perp\\!\\!\\perp" --- ## Agenda - Review from last time - IPW formulation of the g-formula - IPW estimators - Assessing and responding to positivity violations - Other propensity-based methods - regression - stratification - matching ## Review Two equivalent ways of representing the g-formula... $$\mathbb{E}[Y^a] = \mathbb{E}\Big[\mathbb{E}[Y \mid A=a, L]\Big] = \mathbb{E}\Big[Y \frac{I(A=a)}{P(A=a \mid L)}\Big]$$. ## Review Motivating two different ways of leveraging parametric models: - $logit(P(Y=1 \mid A=a, L=l)) = \theta_0 + \theta_1a + \theta_2l+\theta_3al$ - $logit(P(A=1 \mid L=l)) = \eta_0 + \eta_1l$ - $$\begin{align} & \mathbb{E}[Y^{a=1}] \\ = & \mathbb{E}\Big[expit(\theta_0 + \theta_1 + \theta_2L+\theta_3L)\Big] \\ = &\mathbb{E}\Big[Y \frac{I(A=1)}{expit(\eta_0 + \eta_1L)}\Big]\end{align}$$ ## Review Motivating two different types of estimators: - $\frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n expit(\hat\theta_0 + \hat\theta_1(a=1) + \hat\theta_2L+\hat\theta_3(a=1)L_i) \to \mathbb{E}[Y^{a=1}]$ - $\frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n\frac{I(A_i=a=1)}{expit(\hat\eta_0 + \hat\eta_1L_i)} \to \mathbb{E}[Y^{a=1}]$ - Remember, consistency of our estimators depends on modelling assumptions. - **Discussion question**: if you were forced to specify a model for treatment or for the outcome, which would you choose, and why? ## Review IPW clarifies why we need positivity: $$ \mathbb{E}\Big[Y \frac{I(A=a)}{P(A=a \mid L)}\Big]$$ What happens if $P(A=a \mid L) = 0$? ## More IPW intuition $$\begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\Big[Y^{a}\Big] = \mathbb{E}\Big[Y\frac{I(A=a)}{f(A \mid L)}\Big] \end{align*}$$ Radon-Nikodym theorem for a change in measure: Let $P^*$ be some arbitrary law that is different from $P$. According to the Radon-Nykodym theorem we have: $$\mathbb{E}_{\color{red}{P^*}}[Y] = \mathbb{E}_{\color{blue}{P}}\Big[Y \frac{\color{red}{f_{P^*}(Y, A, L)}}{\color{blue}{f_{P}(Y, A, L)}}\Big].$$

We want to change from the factual law to the counterfactual law of $Y$.

## More IPW intuition $$\mathbb{E}[Y^a] \equiv \mathbb{E}_{\color{red}{P^*}}[Y] = \mathbb{E}_{\color{blue}{P}}\Big[Y \frac{\color{red}{f_{P^*}(Y, A, L)}}{\color{blue}{f_{P}(Y, A, L)}}\Big].$$ ## More IPW intuition Let $A^{a}$ denote the variable for the \textit{assigned treatment} under an regime that fixes treatment to $a$.

$$\begin{align}\color{red}{f_{P^*}(y, a', l) = P(Y^{a}=y \mid A^a=a', L^a=l) P(A^a=a' \mid L^a=l) P(L^a=l)}\end{align}$$

$$=\color{blue}{P(Y=y \mid A=a', L=l)} \color{red}{P(A^a=a' \mid L^a=l)} \color{blue}{P(L=l)}$$

## More IPW intuition **Discussion Question**: What is $\color{red}{P(A^{a}=a' \mid L^a=l)}$?

We have $$\color{red}{P(A^{a}=a' \mid L^a=l) = I(a'=a)},$$ i.e., all the probability mass is on the value $a$.

$$\color{red}{f_{P^*}(y, a', l)} = \color{blue}{P(Y=y \mid A=a', L=l)} \color{red}{I(a'=a)} \color{blue}{P(L=l)} $$

$$\color{blue}{f_{P}(y, a', l) = P(Y=y \mid A=a', L=l) f(a' \mid l) P(L=l)}$$

## More IPW intuition So: $$\begin{align*} \frac{\color{red}{f_{P^*}(y, a', l)}}{\color{blue}{f_{P}(y, a', l)}} & = \frac{\color{blue}{P(Y=y \mid A=a', L=l)} \color{red}{I(a'=a)} \color{blue}{P(L=l)}}{\color{blue}{P(Y=y \mid A=a', L=l) f_P(a' \mid l) P(L=l)}} \\ & = \frac{ \color{red}{I(a'=a)}}{\color{blue}{f_P(a' \mid l)}} \end{align*}$$ ## More IPW intuition $$\begin{align*} \mathbb{E}_{\color{red}{P^*}}[Y] = & \mathbb{E}_{\color{blue}{P}}\Big[Y \frac{\color{red}{f_{P^*}(Y, A, L)}}{\color{blue}{f_{P}(Y, A, L)}}\Big] \\ = & \mathbb{E}_{\color{blue}{P}}\Big[Y \frac{\color{red}{I(A=a)}}{\color{blue}{f_P(A \mid L)}}\Big] \end{align*}$$ ## Other Propensity-based methods A classical result: suppose consistency, positivity hold. Define $$\pi(L) = P(A=1 \mid L).$$ If $$Y^a \perp A \mid L$$ then $$Y^a \perp A \mid \pi(L).$$ Implications: we can match, condition, stratify on the propensity score. ## Propensity regression Assume positivity, consistency, exchangeability, and suppose I fit the following regression model: $$\mathbb{E}[Y \mid a, \pi(l)] = \beta_0 + \beta_1a + \beta_2\pi(l).$$ - **Discussion Question**: Does $\beta_1$ have a causal interpretation under these assumptions alone? If not, what additional assumptions are needed? ## Propensity regression What about this model? $$\mathbb{E}[Y \mid a, \pi(l)] = \beta_0 + \beta_1a + \beta_2\pi(l) + \beta_3a\pi(l).$$ **Discussion Question**: Suppose the model is correctly specified. What is the causal interpretation of: - $\beta_1$ - $\beta_1 + \beta_2*(0.5)$ - What are some possible disadvantages of these parameters? ## Propensity stratification When variables are continuous, it is very difficult to correctly specify a parsimonious model for the conditional outcome mean. - We could consider including more and more polynomial terms for $\pi(l)$ and all possible interactions ($K$ large): - $$\mathbb{E}[Y \mid a, \pi(l)] = \beta_0 + \beta_1a + \sum\limits_{j=1}^K (\theta_j\pi(l)^j + \gamma_ja\pi(l)^j).$$ - **Discussion Question**: How would this help? How would this hurt? ## Propensity stratification But what if we took the following approach: - Define $\pi_{3,k}(L)$ to be an indicator variable that an individual's propensity was in the $k^{th}$ tertile of propensity scores, $\pi(L)$ (e.g., $\pi_{3,1}(L) = 1$ if an individual's propensity was in the lowest third of propensities.) - Consider the following model: $$\mathbb{E}[Y \mid a, \pi_{3}(l)] = \beta_0 + \beta_1a + \beta_2\pi_{3,2}(l)+ \beta_3\pi_{3,3}(l) + \beta_4a\pi_{3,2}(l)+ \beta_5a\pi_{3,3}(l).$$ - **Discussion Question**: Is this model correctly specified? - **Discussion Question**: Does $\beta_1$ have a causal interpretation? If not, what additional assumptions are needed? - **Discussion Question**: What are some possible disadvantages of these parameters? ## Propensity stratification When we condition on propensity score *strata*, we can correctly specify models, but we are concerned about residual confounding *within* strata. - We could consider defining smaller and smaller propensity score strata (i.e., instead of tertiles, we could use quartiles, or quintiles, or...) - **Discussion Question**: How would this help? - **Discussion Question**: How would this hurt? ## Propensity matching Consider the following procedure: - For every treated individual ($A=1$) find an untreated individual ($A=0$) with the same$^*$ propensity $\pi(L)$. Suppose there exists a match for all individuals with ($A=1$). Let $\mathcal{B}_n$ denote the set of indices for individuals in the original sample, for whom a match is found. - Consider the following estimator: - $\frac{\sum\limits_{i\in\mathcal{B}_n}I(A_i=1)Y_i}{\sum\limits_{i\in\mathcal{B}_n}I(A_i=1)} - \frac{\sum\limits_{i\in\mathcal{B}_n}I(A_i=0)Y_i}{\sum\limits_{i\in\mathcal{B}_n}I(A_i=0)}.$ - Is this estimator consistent for some causal effect? - Is it the marginal ATE? If not, what kind of ATE is it? ## Propensity matching Matching the treated individuals targets the Average treatment effect **among the treated** (ATT) $$\mathbb{E}[Y^{a=1} \mid A=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y^{a=0} \mid A=1].$$ - **Discussion Question**: How do we interpret this? - How might this effect be useful in practice? - The ATT requires weaker assumptions than the ATE to identify. - **Discussion Question**: Why? ## Propensity matching The ATT requires fewer assumptions because, under consistency, we identify $\mathbb{E}[Y^{a=1} \mid A=1]$ for free. - Partial exchangeability: $Y^{a=0} \perp A \mid L$ - Partial positivity: $P(A=0 \mid L=l)>0$ for all $l$ with positive probability in the *subpopulation* with $A=1$. ## Propensity matching ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} expit <- function(x) exp(x) / (1 + exp(x)) n <- 10000 beta <- c(-1, 1, 0.5) U_L <- runif(n) U_A <- runif(n) U_Y1 <- runif(n) U_Y0 <- runif(n) S <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.7) L <- ifelse(S == 1, qnorm(U_L, 1, 0.75), qnorm(U_L, -3, 0.5)) eta <- c(-2, 1) pi <- ifelse(L < -1, 0, expit(eta[1] + eta[2]*L)) A <- rbinom(n, 1, pi) Y1 <- qnorm(U_Y1, beta[1] + beta[2]*1 + beta[3]*L, 1) Y0 <- qnorm(U_Y0, beta[1] + beta[2]*0 + beta[3]*L, 1) Y <- Y1*A + Y0*(1-A) df2 <- data.frame(L=L, A=A, pi=pi, Y1=Y1, Y0=Y0, Y=Y, S=S) ``` ::: ## Propensity matching ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](unit2-lect5_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Propensity matching ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #Constructing weights for a=1 fit<-glm(A~L + L^2 + L^3 + L^4+ L^5, data=df2, family=binomial(link=logit)) df2$pi<-predict(fit, df2, type="response") df2$W<-df2$A / df2$pi #Truth mean(df2$Y1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.1024334 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} #Horvitz-Thompson Estimator mean(df2$Y*df2$W) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.3366922 ``` ::: ::: ## Propensity matching Nearest neighbor matching: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} treated <- df2[df2$A == 1, ] controls <- df2[df2$A == 0, ] #Constructing weights for a=1 matches <- sapply(treated$pi, function(p) { which.min(abs(controls$pi - p)) }) df_matched<-rbind(treated, controls[matches, ]) ``` ::: ## Propensity matching ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](unit2-lect5_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Propensity matching ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #Truth mean(treated$Y1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.6875912 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(treated$Y0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.2741315 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} #Matched mean(df_matched[df_matched$A==1, ]$Y) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.6875912 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(df_matched[df_matched$A==0, ]$Y) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.3087207 ``` ::: ::: ## Propensity matching Matching the untreated individuals targets the Average treatment effect **among the untreated** (ATU) $$\mathbb{E}[Y^{a=1} \mid A=0] - \mathbb{E}[Y^{a=0} \mid A=0].$$ ## Propensity matching The ATU requires fewer assumptions because, under consistency, we identify $\mathbb{E}[Y^{a=1} \mid A=0]$ for free. - Partial exchangeability: $Y^{a=0} \perp A \mid L$ - Partial positivity: $P(A=1 \mid L=l)>0$ for all $l$ with positive probability in the *subpopulation* with $A=0$. ## ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](unit2-lect5_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## ## Propensity matching Nearest neighbor matching: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} treated <- df3[df3$A == 1, ] controls <- df3[df3$A == 0, ] #Constructing weights for a=1 matches <- sapply(controls$pi, function(p) { which.min(abs(treated$pi - p)) }) df_matched<-rbind(controls, treated[matches, ]) ``` ::: ## ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](unit2-lect5_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Matching will fail when the positivity conditions fail! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #Truth mean(controls$Y1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.3025387 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(controls$Y0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -1.291546 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} #Matched mean(df_matched[df_matched$A==1, ]$Y) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.3074853 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(df_matched[df_matched$A==0, ]$Y) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -1.291546 ``` ::: ::: ## Propensity-score methods summary - All methods require the same three usual assumptions. - Propensity-score regression methods - When we are able to correctly specify the outcome model, we identify causal effects, but... - simple models rarely identify causal effects (residual confounding from model misspecification) - complex models complicate interpretation (conditional effects) and estimation (curse of dimensionality) ## Propensity-score methods summary - Propensity matching methods - Require weaker positivity and exchangeability assumptions but... - different matching strategies lead to different estimands with different interpretations - perfect matches (almost) never exist when $L$ is continuous, so must specify a matching method.

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
